title: A Comparative Study of the Physics-Informed Neural Networks and the Nonstandard Finite Difference Methods for the Solution of the Two-Dimensional Fisher-KPP Reaction-Diffusion Equation
content: This study presents a comparative investigation of a Nonstandard Finite Difference (NSFD) method and a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) for the numerical solution of the two-dimensional nonlinear Fisher–KPP reaction–diffusion equation. The NSFD scheme incorporates a nonstandard temporal denominator, a nonlocal treatment of the nonlinear reaction term, and mixed time levels, while the PINN approximates the solution by minimizing a physics-informed loss constructed from the governing equation and the prescribed initial and boundary conditions. The reference traveling-wave solution is not used as interior training data for the PINN or in the NSFD interior update, but is employed independently for numerical validation. Theoretical analysis of the NSFD scheme establishes positivity, preservation of the invariant interval [0, 1], consistency, linearized stability, and convergence. In particular, first-order max-norm convergence is established along the refinement path ∆x = ∆y = h and ∆t = h3. Numerical grid-refinement and invariant-region experiments are consistent with these theoretical results. The PINN is trained using a two-stage Adam–L-BFGS optimization procedure and subsequently evaluated independently against the reference solution. The numerical comparison shows that both methods successfully approximate the spatial and temporal behavior of the reference solution. However, under the computational settings considered, the PINN produces smaller RMSE, MAE, maximum absolute error, and relative L2 error than the NSFD method, thereby providing a more accurate approximation of the benchmark. The computational comparison reveals a complementary trade-off: the NSFD method provides a substantially less expensive direct time-marching solution, whereas the PINN incurs a considerably higher initial training cost but enables rapid post-training evaluation. These results demonstrate that, for the present Fisher–KPP benchmark, the PINN performs better in terms of numerical accuracy, while the NSFD method offers lower direct computational cost together with analytically established structure-preserving and convergence properties.
